fr.text: She ___ to school every day.
fr.explanation: Présent simple, 3e personne du singulier : on ajoute -s ou -es au verbe (she goes). « Every day » indique une habitude.

fr.text: I ___ my homework yesterday.
fr.explanation: « Yesterday » situe l'action dans un passé terminé : on emploie le prétérit (did). Le present perfect ne s'emploie pas avec un repère passé précis.

fr.text: She has lived in Rabat ___ 2015.
fr.explanation: « Since » + point de départ (since 2015) ; « for » + durée (for ten years). Avec le present perfect : She has lived here since 2015.

fr.text: If I ___ rich, I would travel around the world.
fr.explanation: Conditionnel de type 2 (hypothèse irréelle dans le présent) : If + prétérit, would + base verbale. En anglais soigné, on emploie « were » à toutes les personnes (« was » est courant à l'oral). « Will » et « would » ne s'emploient pas dans la subordonnée en « if ».

fr.text: If it rains tomorrow, we ___ at home.
fr.explanation: Conditionnel de type 1 (situation possible) : If + présent simple, will + base verbale.

fr.text: If you had studied harder, you ___ the exam last year.
fr.explanation: Conditionnel de type 3 (hypothèse irréelle portant sur le passé) : If + past perfect, would have + participe passé. « Last year » situe le résultat dans le passé, ce qui exclut « would pass ».

fr.text: Rabat is ___ capital of Morocco.
fr.explanation: L'article défini « the » désigne un élément unique ou précisément identifié : un pays n'a qu'une capitale, d'où « the capital of Morocco ». « A/an » présenterait la capitale comme une parmi d'autres.

fr.text: Choose the correct sentence.
choices: There are much students in the classroom.
There are many students in the classroom.
There is many students in the classroom.
There have many students in the classroom.
fr.correction: « There are many students in the classroom. »
fr.explanation: « There are » + nom pluriel. « Many » s'emploie avec les noms dénombrables (many students), « much » avec les indénombrables (much water).

fr.text: The letter ___ by the manager last week.
fr.explanation: Voix passive au prétérit : was/were + participe passé. « Last week » impose le passé.

fr.text: English ___ in many countries.
fr.explanation: Voix passive au présent simple : am/is/are + participe passé (speak → spoken).

fr.text: He is the man ___ car was stolen.
fr.explanation: « Whose » exprime la possession (l'homme dont la voiture a été volée). « Who » renvoie à une personne sujet, « which » à une chose.

fr.text: When I arrived, they ___ dinner.
fr.explanation: Past continuous (was/were + V-ing) pour une action en cours au moment où une autre action passée (arrived) se produit.

fr.text: My sister is ___ than me.
fr.explanation: Comparatif des adjectifs courts : adjectif + -er + than. Avec les adjectifs longs : more + adjectif (more interesting).

fr.text: This is the ___ film I have ever seen.
fr.explanation: Superlatif des adjectifs longs : the most + adjectif. « Ever » accompagne souvent le superlatif.

fr.text: You ___ wear a seatbelt; it's the law.
fr.explanation: « Must » exprime l'obligation. « Might » exprime une faible probabilité et « can » la capacité ou la permission.

fr.text: I look forward to ___ from you.
fr.explanation: Dans « look forward to », « to » est une préposition : elle est suivie de la forme en -ing. Formule très courante en fin de lettre ou d'e-mail.

fr.text: She is used to ___ early.
fr.explanation: « Be used to + V-ing » signifie « être habitué à ». À ne pas confondre avec « used to + base verbale », qui exprime une habitude passée révolue (I used to smoke).

fr.text: He asked me where ___.
fr.explanation: Au discours indirect, la question perd l'inversion et l'auxiliaire « do », et les temps reculent : « Where do you live? » devient « He asked me where I lived ».

fr.text: How ___ money do you have?
fr.explanation: « Money » est indénombrable : how much. On emploie « how many » avec un nom dénombrable au pluriel (how many books).

fr.text: By the time we got to the station, the train ___.
fr.explanation: Le past perfect (had + participe passé) exprime une action antérieure à une autre action passée (got to the station).

fr.text: Hardly ___ the house when it started to rain.
fr.explanation: Après un adverbe restrictif placé en tête de phrase (hardly, scarcely, no sooner, never), on inverse le sujet et l'auxiliaire. « Hardly… when » exprime l'antériorité immédiate dans le passé et se construit avec le past perfect : Hardly had I left the house when it started to rain.

fr.text: I wish I ___ speak Chinese.
fr.explanation: « I wish » + prétérit exprime un souhait irréel ou un regret dans le présent : I wish I could speak Chinese (j'aimerais savoir parler chinois).

fr.text: They ___ football right now.
fr.explanation: Présent continu (be + V-ing) pour une action en cours au moment où l'on parle (right now).

fr.text: She suggested ___ to the museum.
fr.explanation: « Suggest » est suivi de la forme en -ing ou de « that + sujet + base verbale ». On ne dit pas « suggest to go ».

fr.text: What is the opposite of "expensive"?
fr.explanation: Expensive (cher) s'oppose à cheap (bon marché). Costly est un synonyme d'expensive.

fr.text: Choose the synonym of "huge".
fr.explanation: Huge = enormous = immense. Tiny signifie « minuscule ».

fr.text: A person who designs buildings is called an ___.
fr.explanation: L'architect (architecte) conçoit les bâtiments. L'optician est l'opticien, l'electrician l'électricien et l'accountant le comptable.

fr.text: What does "to apply for a job" mean?
choices: To formally ask to be considered for a job
fr.explanation: Apply for a job = poser sa candidature. Leave ou resign = quitter son poste ; be promoted = obtenir une promotion ; hire = embaucher.

fr.text: Complete: "The company's profits ___ by 20% last year."
fr.explanation: « Increase » est ici intransitif (les bénéfices ont augmenté). « Raise » est transitif (raise prices) ; « grow up » signifie grandir, pour une personne ; « rise » seul conviendrait (profits rose by 20%), mais pas « rise up », qui signifie se soulever ou s'élever.

fr.text: Complete with the right verb: "I need to ___ a decision."
fr.explanation: Collocations : make a decision, make a mistake, make money ; do homework, do business, do one's best. L'anglais britannique accepte aussi « take a decision ».

fr.text: What is a "deadline"?
choices: The latest time by which something must be done
The end of a phone call
A dangerous line on the road
fr.explanation: Deadline = date ou heure limite. Exemple : The application deadline is 16 October.

fr.text: "Actually" means:
fr.explanation: Faux ami : « actually » signifie « en fait, en réalité » et non « actuellement », qui se dit currently ou at present.

fr.text: "Eventually" means:
fr.explanation: Faux ami : eventually = finalement, à la longue. « Éventuellement » se traduit par possibly ou if necessary.

fr.text: Which word means "a person who travels to another country for pleasure"?
fr.explanation: Un tourist voyage pour le loisir. Immigrant : personne qui s'installe dans un autre pays ; refugee : personne qui fuit un danger ; citizen : citoyen.

fr.text: The plural of "child" is:
fr.explanation: Pluriels irréguliers courants : child → children, man → men, woman → women, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, mouse → mice.

fr.text: The past participle of "write" is:
fr.explanation: Verbe irrégulier : write – wrote – written.

fr.text: The simple past of "go" is:
fr.explanation: Verbe irrégulier : go – went – gone.

fr.text: Neither my brother ___ my sister likes coffee.
fr.explanation: Corrélations : neither… nor (ni… ni) ; either… or (soit… soit).

fr.text: You're coming tonight, ___?
fr.explanation: Question tag : on reprend l'auxiliaire de la phrase (are) à la forme négative quand la phrase est affirmative, avec le même sujet (you).

fr.text: ___ the rain, the match continued.
fr.explanation: Despite / in spite of + nom ou V-ing. Although / even though + proposition (Although it was raining, …). However est un adverbe de liaison.

fr.text: "The meeting has been postponed." This means that the meeting:
fr.explanation: Postpone = put off = reporter à plus tard. Annuler se dit cancel.

fr.text: "Applicants must hold a baccalaureate in science." Who can apply?
choices: Only students currently in high school
Only people who have a science baccalaureate
Anyone, with or without a baccalaureate
fr.correction: Seuls les titulaires d'un bac scientifique.
fr.explanation: « Must hold » = doivent être titulaires de ; « applicants » = les candidats.

fr.text: Which word is closest in meaning to "skills"?
fr.explanation: Skills = compétences, savoir-faire. Salaries = salaires ; diplomas = diplômes ; hobbies = loisirs.

fr.text: In a hotel, the "front desk" is:
fr.explanation: Front desk = reception desk : c'est là que l'on fait le check-in et le check-out.

fr.text: It's high time we ___.
fr.explanation: « It's (high) time + sujet + prétérit » signifie qu'une action aurait déjà dû avoir lieu : It's high time we left (il est grand temps de partir).

fr.text: He has been working here ___ ten years.
fr.explanation: For + durée (ten years) ; since + point de départ ; « ago » s'emploie avec le prétérit (ten years ago).

fr.text: Which sentence is correct?
choices: I have waited since two hours.
I am waiting since two hours.
I have been waiting for two hours.
fr.correction: « I have been waiting for two hours. »
fr.explanation: Pour une action commencée dans le passé et qui dure encore, on emploie le present perfect (souvent continu) avec for + durée. « Since two hours » est un calque fautif du français.

fr.text: The more you practise, ___ you become.
fr.explanation: Structure « the + comparatif…, the + comparatif… » : the more…, the better… (plus…, plus…).

fr.text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "The lawyer charged a very high … for his services."
fr.explanation: A fee is the money paid for professional services (a lawyer, a doctor, school fees). A fare is the price of a journey (a bus fare); a debt is money owed.

fr.text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "The sun was so strong that the curtains … from dark blue to light grey."
fr.explanation: Colours fade when they lose their intensity over time. To faint means to lose consciousness; paled is used for faces; bleached suggests a deliberate chemical whitening.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "I'm looking forward to … you next week."
fr.explanation: In "look forward to", "to" is a preposition, so it is followed by a gerund (-ing form): "I look forward to hearing from you."

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "Would you mind … the window? It's cold in here."
fr.explanation: "Would you mind" is always followed by the -ing form. The same applies to verbs such as enjoy, avoid, finish and suggest.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "His eyes were … tired that he couldn't read the text."
fr.explanation: "So + adjective + that" expresses a consequence. "Such" is used with a noun ("such a tiring day that…"); "too" would require "to" + infinitive ("too tired to read").

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "By the time we arrived at the station, the train …"
fr.explanation: The past perfect describes an action completed before another past action ("we arrived"). The present perfect cannot be used with a past reference point.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "If I … more time, I would learn another language."
fr.explanation: The second conditional (an imaginary present situation) uses "if" + past simple, then "would" + base verb. "Will" and "would" are not used in the if-clause.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "She has been working for this company … 2019."
fr.explanation: "Since" introduces a starting point (since 2019, since Monday); "for" introduces a duration (for six years). Both are used with the present perfect.

fr.text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "The company needs to decide once and … what its position is."
fr.explanation: "Once and for all" is a fixed expression meaning "definitively, finally". "For good" also means permanently, but it is not used after "once and".

fr.text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "Don't put your glass on the … of the table; it might fall."
fr.explanation: The edge is the outer limit of an object (the edge of a table, of a cliff). A border separates countries; a boundary marks the limit of an area.

fr.text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "There's a problem with my car: one of the tyres is …"
fr.explanation: A flat tyre has lost its air. This collocation is the standard one; "depressed" describes a person's mood.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "The report … by the manager before the meeting started."
fr.explanation: The report does not act: the passive voice is needed (be + past participle). The past perfect passive shows that the approval happened before the meeting started.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "Neither the students nor the teacher … aware of the change."
fr.explanation: With "neither… nor", the verb agrees with the nearest subject: "the teacher" is singular. With "Neither the teacher nor the students", we would say "were".

fr.text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "When there is a doubt, the examiner's decision is …"
fr.explanation: A decision that cannot be changed or appealed is "final" ("The referee's decision is final"). "Definite" means clear or certain, but it is not used in this fixed expression.

fr.text: Read the sentence: "Teachers who are more open to new ideas tend to produce students with greater intellectual flexibility." It can be inferred that:
choices: Open-minded teaching helps students think more flexibly
New ideas are harmful in the classroom
Students' flexibility does not depend on their teachers
Strict teachers always produce the best students
fr.correction: The teacher's openness supports the students' flexibility.
fr.explanation: The sentence establishes a link between the teachers' openness and the students' intellectual flexibility. The other options contradict it or are not supported by it. Inference questions ask what the text implies, not what we think.

fr.text: Read the sentence: "In a group of five, there are five people doing the same thing: every idea must be understood by four others." The main idea is that:
choices: Communication becomes more complex as the group grows
Groups of five are always inefficient
Only two people can really communicate
fr.correction: The more members, the more complex communication becomes.
fr.explanation: The sentence compares a pair with a group of five to show that each message must reach and be understood by more people. It does not say that groups of five are inefficient, nor that large groups are faster.

fr.text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "I'm sorry, I didn't … to disturb you."
fr.explanation: "I didn't mean to…" expresses that something was not intentional. It is a very common way to apologise in English.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "Hardly … the room when the phone rang."
fr.explanation: When a negative adverb such as hardly, scarcely, no sooner or never begins the sentence, the subject and the auxiliary are inverted: "Hardly had he entered the room when the phone rang."

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "She … to school every day."
fr.explanation: In the present simple, the third person singular (he, she, it) takes -s or -es: she goes, he watches, it works.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "Look! The children … in the garden."
fr.explanation: "Look!" shows that the action is happening now: we use the present continuous (be + -ing).

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "I … my homework yesterday evening."
fr.explanation: "Yesterday evening" is a finished time in the past: we use the past simple. The present perfect cannot be used with a finished past time expression.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "I … in Rabat since 2020."
fr.explanation: "Since" + a starting point shows an action that began in the past and continues now: present perfect (or present perfect continuous: have been living).

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "While I … TV, the phone rang."
fr.explanation: The past continuous describes an action in progress (watching TV) interrupted by a shorter action in the past simple (the phone rang).

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "Look at those clouds! It … rain."
fr.explanation: "Be going to" is used for predictions based on present evidence (the clouds). "Will" is used for spontaneous decisions and general predictions.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "Casablanca is … city in Morocco."
fr.explanation: The superlative of a short adjective is "the + adjective + -est". The comparative "larger than" compares two things.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "This exam was … than the last one."
fr.explanation: Long adjectives (two or more syllables, except those ending in -y) form the comparative with "more": more difficult, more expensive.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "He is not … to drive a car."
fr.explanation: "Enough" comes after an adjective (old enough) but before a noun (enough money).

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "If it rains tomorrow, we … at home."
fr.explanation: First conditional (a real possibility in the future): if + present simple, then will + base verb.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "If I had studied harder, I … the exam."
fr.explanation: Third conditional (an imaginary past situation): if + past perfect, then would have + past participle. It expresses regret or criticism about the past.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "The new hospital … next year."
fr.explanation: The hospital does not build itself: the passive voice is needed. Future passive: will be + past participle.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "English … in many countries."
fr.explanation: Present simple passive: am/is/are + past participle. The agent (by people) is not mentioned because it is obvious.

fr.text: Choose the correct relative pronoun: "The student … won the prize is my cousin."
fr.explanation: "Who" refers to people and is the subject of the relative clause. "Which" refers to things; "whose" shows possession.

fr.text: Choose the correct relative pronoun: "That's the man … car was stolen."
fr.explanation: "Whose" expresses possession (his car was stolen). It can refer to people or things.

fr.text: Report the sentence: She said, "I am tired."
choices: She said that I am tired.
She said that she is tired yesterday.
She said that she was tired.
She said she has been tired tomorrow.
fr.correction: She said that she was tired.
fr.explanation: In reported speech, after a reporting verb in the past, the tense moves back (am → was) and pronouns change (I → she).

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "You … wear a seat belt. It's the law."
fr.explanation: "Must" expresses an obligation. "Mustn't" expresses a prohibition; "needn't" means it is not necessary.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "She can't be at home; I … her at the library five minutes ago."
fr.explanation: "Five minutes ago" is a finished past time: past simple. "Can't be" expresses a logical deduction (impossibility).

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "There isn't … milk left in the fridge."
fr.explanation: "Any" is used in negative and interrogative sentences. "Milk" is uncountable, so "many" and "a few" are not possible.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "How … money do you need?"
fr.explanation: "Much" is used with uncountable nouns (money, water, information); "many" with countable nouns (books, students).

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "He decided … abroad after his graduation."
fr.explanation: Some verbs are followed by the infinitive: decide, want, hope, plan, agree, refuse. Others take the -ing form: enjoy, avoid, finish, mind.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "She is interested … economics."
fr.explanation: Fixed preposition: interested in, good at, afraid of, responsible for, depend on.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "We arrived … the airport at 6 a.m."
fr.explanation: We say "arrive at" a building or a precise place (the airport, the station) and "arrive in" a city or a country (arrive in Rabat).

fr.text: Choose the correct question tag: "You're a student, …?"
fr.explanation: A question tag uses the same auxiliary as the sentence, in the opposite form: positive sentence → negative tag (You are… aren't you?).

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "I wish I … more time to prepare."
fr.explanation: "Wish" + past simple expresses a regret about the present (I don't have enough time). For a regret about the past: I wish I had had more time.

fr.text: What is the opposite of "expensive"?
fr.explanation: Expensive means "costing a lot of money"; cheap (or inexpensive) is its opposite. Costly is a synonym.

fr.text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "The company made a big … last year: its income was much higher than its costs."
fr.explanation: A profit is the money earned after paying all costs. A loss is the opposite; a debt is money owed; a budget is a financial plan.

fr.text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "She sent her … to several companies to find a job."
fr.explanation: A CV (in American English, a résumé) presents your education and experience. An invoice is a bill for goods or services; a receipt proves that you paid.

fr.text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "The bank offers a low interest rate on this … ."
fr.explanation: A loan is money that is borrowed. "Lend" (give) and "borrow" (receive) are verbs; "lent" is the past of lend.

fr.text: Which word means "a person who buys goods or services"?
fr.explanation: A supplier provides goods to a company, an employee works for it, and a shareholder owns part of it.

fr.text: Choose the correct phrasal verb: "Please … the form and give it to the secretary."
fr.explanation: "Give up" = stop trying; "look after" = take care of; "turn down" = refuse or reduce the volume.

fr.text: Choose the correct phrasal verb: "He was offered a job in Dubai, but he … it … because of his family."
fr.explanation: "Turn down an offer" means refuse it. "Put off" means postpone.

fr.text: Choose the correct phrasal verb: "The meeting has been … until next Monday."
fr.explanation: "Put on" = wear or switch on; "take off" = remove (clothes) or leave the ground (a plane); "set up" = create or establish.

fr.text: Which word is a synonym of "begin"?
fr.explanation: Begin, start and commence have the same meaning. Finish, stop and end are antonyms.

fr.text: Choose the correct word: "This decision will have a positive … on the economy."
fr.explanation: "Effect" is usually a noun (a result); "affect" is a verb (to influence): the decision will affect the economy.

fr.text: Choose the correct word: "The … of the population lives in cities."
fr.explanation: "The majority of" means most of. A "mayor" is the head of a town council.

fr.text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "Climate change is one of the most … issues of our time."
fr.explanation: A pressing issue is an urgent problem that must be dealt with quickly.

fr.text: Choose the correct collocation: "to … a decision"
fr.explanation: We "make" a decision, a mistake, a plan, money; we "do" homework, a job, business. ("Take a decision" is also used in British English.)

fr.text: Choose the correct collocation: "Students must … their homework before Friday."
fr.explanation: We "do" homework, exercises, research and the shopping, but we "make" an effort or a mistake.

fr.text: What does the idiom "a piece of cake" mean?
fr.explanation: "The test was a piece of cake" means it was very easy. Other idioms: "break the ice" (start a conversation), "under the weather" (slightly ill).

fr.text: Read: "Despite the heavy rain, the match was not cancelled." This means that:
choices: The match took place although it was raining heavily
The match was cancelled because of the rain
It did not rain during the match
fr.explanation: "Despite" (+ noun) expresses contrast, like "although" (+ clause): although it was raining heavily, the match was not cancelled.

fr.text: Read: "Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus." This means:
choices: If you hurry, you will miss the bus
You will miss the bus anyway
You hurried and caught the bus
If you don't hurry, you will miss the bus
fr.explanation: "Unless" introduces a negative condition: unless you hurry = if you don't hurry.

fr.text: Read: "Morocco's renewable energy share has grown steadily, mainly thanks to solar and wind projects." The main idea is that:
choices: Morocco has stopped using fossil fuels
Solar and wind power have helped increase the share of renewable energy in Morocco
Wind projects have failed in Morocco
Renewable energy has decreased in Morocco
fr.correction: Growth driven by solar and wind.
fr.explanation: "Has grown steadily" means it has increased regularly, and "mainly thanks to" gives the main causes. The text says nothing about stopping fossil fuels.

fr.text: Read: "The author argues that small classes improve learning, although critics point out their high cost." The word "although" introduces:
fr.explanation: Although, though, even though, whereas and however introduce an opposing idea. Consequence: so, therefore; cause: because, since; example: for instance.

fr.text: In the sentence "The firm hired fifty new employees last month", the word "hired" means:
fr.explanation: To hire is to give someone a job. Its opposite is to fire (or dismiss, lay off).

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "Not only … the exam, but she also got the highest mark."
fr.explanation: When a negative or restrictive expression (not only, never, rarely, hardly) starts the sentence, the auxiliary comes before the subject: Not only did she pass…

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "He used to … football when he was a child."
fr.explanation: "Used to" + infinitive describes a past habit that no longer exists. "Be used to + -ing" means "be accustomed to".

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "Neither of the two answers … correct."
fr.explanation: "Neither of" + plural noun normally takes a singular verb in formal English: neither of them is correct.

fr.text: Choose the correct option: "It's high time we … for the exam."
fr.explanation: "It's time / It's high time" + subject + past simple expresses that something should already be happening: It's high time we started.

fr.text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "The government plans to … unemployment by creating new jobs."
fr.explanation: To reduce unemployment is to lower it. "Raise" means increase, "reject" refuse, "remain" stay.
